item.title: PSBTs: How Several Devices Sign One Bitcoin Payment
item.description: What a PSBT (partially signed bitcoin transaction) is, what's inside one, how it moves between devices by USB, QR or file, and what each signer must check.
item.content:encoded:
If you've used a hardware wallet with desktop software, or set up a multisig wallet, you've met the letters PSBT, often as a file to save, a QR code to scan or a step called "export the transaction". It stands for Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction, and it's the reason a payment can be built on one device, signed on another, co-signed on a third, and broadcast from a fourth, without any of them sharing a private key. This post explains what a PSBT is, what's inside one, how it travels, and what each device should check before it signs.

The problem a PSBT solves

A bitcoin transaction says "spend these coins, send this much here and the rest back to me", and it needs a valid signature for each coin it spends. In a simple software wallet, one program does everything: picks the coins, builds the transaction, signs it with the key it holds, and broadcasts it.

That breaks down as soon as the key lives somewhere else. A hardware wallet holds the key but has no internet connection and doesn't know which coins you own. A multisig wallet needs signatures from two or more devices, often in different places. Each signer needs to see the same proposed transaction, plus enough information to check it and to sign it, and somebody has to collect the signatures at the end.

Before PSBTs, every wallet and device maker solved this its own way, and the formats didn't talk to each other. BIP 174 defined one common format in 2017, and today it's what nearly every wallet and hardware device uses to pass unsigned and partly signed transactions around.

What's inside a PSBT

A PSBT is a small binary file, often shown as base64 text. It holds:

  • The unsigned transaction: which coins (inputs) it spends and which addresses (outputs) it pays, with the amounts.
  • For each input, what a signer needs to know. That includes the coin being spent: its amount and script, and often the whole earlier transaction that created it. It also includes, for multisig, the script that says which keys may sign.
  • Derivation hints: for each key involved, the fingerprint of the device it belongs to and the path to it. A hardware wallet uses these to find its own key, and to recognise which outputs are its own change.
  • Signatures, as they are added, one per key per input.

What it never holds is a private key. A PSBT is safe to pass through a computer, a phone, a USB stick or a QR code: the worst a tampered PSBT can do is ask a device to sign something wrong, which is exactly what the device's screen is there to catch.

The life of a PSBT

BIP 174 describes the work as a set of roles. One program often plays several of them, but the steps are always the same.

  1. Create. The wallet software (the coordinator) picks the coins, the payment and the change, and writes the unsigned transaction into a new PSBT.
  2. Update. It adds what signers will need: the coins' details, the multisig script, the key paths.
  3. Sign. Each signing device reads the PSBT, shows you what it's about to approve, and adds its signature. In a 2-of-3 multisig, two devices do this, one after the other or in parallel.
  4. Combine. If devices signed separate copies, the coordinator merges them into one PSBT with all the signatures.
  5. Finalise. Once enough signatures are in, it assembles them into the exact form the network expects for that script.
  6. Extract and broadcast. It turns the PSBT into an ordinary signed transaction and sends it to the network.

A later standard, BIP 370 ("PSBT version 2"), changes how the transaction is stored inside the file so inputs and outputs can still be added after creation, which helps when several people build one transaction together. Most single-owner wallets still use the original version, and the ideas above apply to both.

How a PSBT travels

Because a PSBT is just data, it can move between devices in whatever way they share:

  • A cable or Bluetooth. The device and the app talk directly; you only see the confirmation on the device.
  • A file. Save it to a microSD card or USB stick, put it in the device, sign, and bring the signed file back.
  • QR codes. The app shows the PSBT as a QR code, the device's camera reads it, and the device shows the signed result as a QR code for the app to read. A PSBT is often too large for a single QR code, so it's split into an animated series. Two formats are common: Blockchain Commons' UR and Coinkite's BBQr (both checked November 2026).
  • NFC. Some devices let you tap the phone against them to pass the PSBT across.

Signing over QR codes or files is called air-gapped signing: the signing device never connects to anything, so the only thing that crosses to it is the PSBT itself, which you can see and check.

The way the PSBT travels doesn't change what's signed. A signature commits to the transaction itself, so a PSBT that's altered in transit either fails to verify or shows the change on the device's screen.

What a signer must check

The device's screen is the only part of the process you can trust when the computer or phone might be compromised. Before you approve, check:

  • Every output's address and amount, against a copy of the address you trust. Read it on the device, not on the computer: start, middle and end.
  • The fee. A fee that's a large share of the payment is a reason to stop.
  • The change. It should be marked as change, or hidden, because the device can prove it returns to your wallet. For multisig, that proof needs the wallet registered on the device. If an output appears that you don't recognise, don't sign.

There's also a check you mostly can't see, done by the device itself: are the input amounts real? The fee is the inputs minus the outputs, so a device that can't trust the input amounts can't trust the fee it shows you. For the older segwit script types used by most multisig wallets today, a signature doesn't commit to the amounts of the other inputs. A malicious coordinator could, in principle, lie about amounts across two signing rounds and turn a modest fee into a huge one. The defence is to include each input's whole previous transaction in the PSBT, so the signer can check the amounts against the transaction ID itself. Many wallets and devices now include or ask for it.

Common problems

  • "Unknown input" or "can't sign". The device doesn't recognise any of its own keys in the PSBT. It's the wrong device, or the wallet is set up with a different key or path.
  • The device warns that change can't be verified. For multisig, the wallet probably isn't registered on that device. Register it from the descriptor and check the first address. What a wallet descriptor is explains what it contains.
  • The PSBT is "missing UTXO data". The coordinator didn't include the previous transactions the device wants. Updating the wallet software usually fixes it.
  • A signed PSBT won't finalise. Not enough valid signatures yet, or two signatures from the same key. Check which devices actually signed.

How Trikey uses PSBTs

Trikey is an open-source 2-of-3 wallet in which you hold all three keys: a hardware wallet, your phone, and either the Trikey Guardian on your own home server or a printed Recovery Key. Every payment is a PSBT passed between them.

  • The phone is the coordinator. It builds the PSBT and signs with key 2. It then reaches the second signer, a hardware wallet over Bluetooth, USB-C or NFC, or an air-gapped device by animated QR (UR or BBQr) (mobile app, hardware wallets by feature). Or it sends the PSBT to the guardian over encrypted nostr messages (protocol).
  • The guardian checks before it co-signs. It rebuilds every input's script from the wallet's descriptor, and it requires each input's full previous transaction and checks it against the transaction ID, the defence described above. It co-signs a phone payment only within the daily limit you set (rules the guardian enforces).
  • The vault is a standard script. wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) on BIP 48 paths, so any multisig-capable wallet can build and sign PSBTs for it without Trikey (design decisions).

Choosing a hardware wallet for multisig compares what different devices show when they sign.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Try it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you use mainnet anyway, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide explains how.

FAQ

Is a PSBT file dangerous to share?

It holds no private keys, so it can't be used to spend on its own. It does reveal the coins and addresses involved, so treat it as private, like a bank statement.

Can someone change a PSBT after I sign it?

They can change the file, but not usefully: your signature covers the transaction's inputs and outputs, so any change to those makes the signature invalid.

Do I need a PSBT for a single-key hardware wallet?

You're using one already. Most desktop and mobile apps pass a PSBT to the device behind the scenes, even when it's plugged in by cable.

What's the difference between a PSBT and a raw transaction?

A raw transaction is the finished, fully signed thing the network accepts. A PSBT is the work-in-progress around it: the same transaction plus the information signers need, and the signatures collected so far.

Why does my air-gapped device show an animated QR code?

The PSBT is larger than one QR code can hold, so it's split into frames. Hold the camera steady until every frame has been read; the order doesn't matter.

item.title: How to Check a Bitcoin Address on Your Hardware Wallet
item.description: How to verify a bitcoin address before sending or sharing it: what the hardware wallet's screen proves, what it can't, and a short routine that catches swaps.
item.category: how to verify a bitcoin address before sending
item.content:encoded:
A bitcoin payment can't be reversed. If the address is wrong, the coins are gone, and the most common way for an address to be wrong is not a typo but a swap: malware, a poisoned transaction history or a tampered web page puts someone else's address where yours should be. A hardware wallet's screen is the tool that catches it, but only if you know what to look at and what that screen can and can't prove. This post walks through both directions, receiving and sending, and ends with a routine short enough to use every time.

Why the computer or phone screen isn't enough

Your computer or phone runs a lot of software: the browser, extensions, the wallet app, whatever else is installed. Any of it, if malicious, can change what you see. Three well-known tricks:

  • Clipboard swapping. Malware watches the clipboard. When you copy something that looks like a bitcoin address, it replaces it with the attacker's. You paste, glance at the first few characters, and send.
  • Address poisoning. An attacker sends a tiny payment from an address that starts and ends like one you use, so it appears in your history. Later you copy "the usual address" from the list and get theirs.
  • A tampered page or app. A fake or compromised wallet app shows a receive address that isn't yours at all.

A hardware wallet is a separate small computer with its own screen. Its software derives addresses from your keys itself, so what it displays doesn't depend on the computer it's plugged into. Trezor calls this the Trusted Display and makes the point plainly: it shows the address the device itself generated, or the transaction it's about to sign. It can't tell you whether an address someone else gave you is the right one. (Checked November 2026.)

That one sentence sets out the whole job. On the receiving side, the device can prove an address is yours. On the sending side, it can only prove what you're about to sign, and you must check that against something you trust.

Receiving: prove the address is yours

Before you hand out an address, or send coins to yourself from an exchange, show it on the device.

  1. In your wallet app, open Receive and choose the option to show or verify the address on the device. Wording varies: "Show on device", "Verify address", "Display address".
  2. The device displays the address. Compare it character by character with what the app shows, or at least the first eight, the last eight and a stretch in the middle. Attackers can generate addresses that match the start and end; matching the middle too is much harder.
  3. Confirm on the device only if they match. If they don't, stop: something between the device and the screen is lying.
  4. Share the address from the app as usual, then compare once more where it lands (the exchange's withdrawal form, the message you're sending), because clipboard malware strikes after the check.

Some devices can also show the address as a QR code on their own screen, so the other party can scan it from the device itself.

Multisig: register the wallet first

For a single-key wallet the device can derive the address alone. A multisig address is built from several keys, so the device needs to know the other keys too. Devices that support it let you register the multisig wallet once: you import the wallet's setup (its descriptor or a setup file), the device shows the details for you to approve, and stores them. Blockstream's guide to registering a multisig on Jade describes how registration then lets the device verify receive addresses and check change automatically when signing.

Two practical points:

  • Check the first address on every device. In a 2-of-3, each device that can display multisig addresses should show the same first receive address. A device that shows a different one has a different picture of the wallet, and that is exactly the kind of mismatch you want to find before any coins arrive. 2-of-3 multisig explained covers why each key matters.
  • Write the first address down with your backup. When you or your heirs restore later, the first address the restored wallet shows should be the same.

Sending: check what you are about to sign

When you pay, the device shows each output of the transaction (the address and the amount) and the fee. It can't know whether the address belongs to the person you mean to pay. Your job is to compare it with a copy you trust.

  1. Get the address from a source the attacker can't easily reach. Best: the recipient's own device screen, read to you, or a second channel. Ask over a call, or confirm in a different app from the one the address came in. For a regular payee, keep the address you verified the first time in a note you control, not in your transaction history.
  2. Compare on the device, not the computer. Read the address on the hardware wallet's screen, character by character, against your trusted copy.
  3. Check the amount and the fee. A fee that's a large share of the payment is a reason to stop.
  4. Check that change returns to you. Most payments have a second output, the change, going back to your own wallet. Good devices mark it as change, or hide it, only when they can prove it's yours: for single-key wallets from the derivation path, for multisig only after the wallet has been registered. If an output you don't recognise appears, or the device can't confirm the change, stop and find out why.
  5. Send a small test first to a new address, if the amount justifies the extra fee. Ask the recipient to confirm it arrived, then send the rest to the same verified address.

Never copy an address from your transaction history. That's exactly where address poisoning puts its look-alikes. Address poisoning and clipboard malware goes deeper into how both attacks work.

What the device can't protect you from

  • A wrong address you approve anyway. If you confirm without reading, the device has done its part.
  • An address that was wrong from the start. If a scammer convinces you their address is your exchange's, the device will faithfully show their address.
  • Addresses the device can't interpret. Some newer address formats are turned into a different-looking output before signing. For example, a silent payment address (sp1…) becomes an ordinary taproot output (bc1p…), so the device can't check it against what you typed. The wallet app should show both so you can compare.
  • A device or firmware you didn't get from the maker. Buy from the manufacturer or an authorised seller, and follow the device's own checks when setting it up.

A one-minute routine

For every payment and every address you share:

  1. Show it on the device.
  2. Compare start, middle and end against your trusted copy.
  3. Check the amount, the fee and the change.
  4. Confirm on the device only if all three match.
  5. For a new payee or a large amount: test first, confirm by a second channel.

That's it. It takes a minute, and it defeats the attacks that empty the most wallets: the ones that never touch your keys, only what you see.

How Trikey handles it

Trikey is an open-source 2-of-3 wallet in which you hold all three keys: a hardware wallet, your phone, and either the Trikey Guardian on your own home server or a printed Recovery Key.

  • Registration and the first address. On devices that need it (Ledger, BitBox02, Jade, Coldcard), the app registers the wallet on the device and shows the first address there (mobile app). For every supported device, the vault's first address is shown on the device's own screen for you to compare (hardware wallets by feature).
  • No address before the device has confirmed one. In Recovery Key mode, the app shows, copies or shares no vault address until the device has shown the first one and you've confirmed it matches. A swapped key export would otherwise put someone else's key in the vault (Recovery Key mode).
  • Limits for the attacks that slip through. If malware gets a phone payment past you, the guardian co-signs phone-only payments only up to a daily limit you set, so, unless you have turned the limit off, a swapped address costs at most that much without the hardware wallet (rules the guardian enforces).

Choosing a hardware wallet for multisig compares what different devices show on screen.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Try it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you use mainnet anyway, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide explains how.

FAQ

Do I need to verify the address every time?

Every time you share a new receive address, and every time you pay. Verification takes seconds, and the attacks it stops are silent: you'd only notice after the coins have left.

Is checking the first and last few characters enough?

Not on its own. Attackers generate look-alike addresses that match the start and end; check a stretch in the middle too, or the whole address for large payments.

My hardware wallet shows a different address from the app. What now?

Don't use either. Disconnect, check you're using the official app from the maker or a trusted source, and try again. If they still differ, assume the computer or phone is compromised and get help from the device maker's support (who will never ask for your seed words).

Can a hardware wallet protect me when I paste an address from an email?

It shows you exactly what you'll pay, so it protects you only if you compare it with a copy you trust. Confirm addresses from emails or chats through a second channel before paying.

Why does my multisig device say it can't verify the change?

Usually because the multisig wallet isn't registered on that device, so it can't prove the change output belongs to you. Register the wallet (most devices take a descriptor or setup file), check the first address, and try again.

item.title: What a Wallet Descriptor Is, and Why Your Heirs Need It
item.description: A multisig wallet descriptor is the map that finds your coins. What it contains, why seed words alone aren't enough, and how to back it up for your heirs.
item.content:encoded:
If you hold bitcoin in a multisig wallet, you've probably been told to "back up the descriptor" as well as your seed words. It sounds like a technical extra. It isn't. For a multisig wallet, the descriptor is what turns a pile of keys back into a wallet with coins in it. Lose it together with one key and recovery can go from an afternoon's work to very hard indeed. This post explains what a descriptor is, reads one line by line, and shows how to store it so that you, or the people who inherit from you, can use it.

The short answer

A wallet descriptor (in full, an output descriptor) is one line of text that describes exactly which addresses belong to a wallet: which public keys are involved, how they are combined, and which script type wraps them. It holds no private keys. It cannot spend anything. But without it, wallet software may not know where to look for your coins.

For a single-key wallet that hardly matters, because the standard paths are few and wallets try them for you. For multisig, it matters a great deal.

Why seed words are not enough for multisig

A seed phrase produces one key. A 2-of-3 multisig wallet's addresses are built from three keys at once: for each address, the wallet takes a public key from each of the three, sorts or orders them, and builds a script that needs two signatures. Change one ingredient and you get a completely different address.

So to find your coins, the software needs to know all three public keys, even if you only have two seeds to sign with. It also needs to know:

  • the script type (for example native segwit P2WSH, or the older nested or legacy forms);
  • how many signatures are required (2 of 3, 3 of 5…);
  • whether the keys are sorted or kept in a fixed order;
  • the derivation path each key came from.

Imagine you hold two seed phrases and the third device is gone. Your two seeds can sign, but they can't tell you the third key's public key. Unless it was written down somewhere, the wallet can't rebuild a single address, and the coins are invisible. They are still there on the blockchain, but you can't find them or spend them.

The descriptor holds all of that in one place. That's why it is sometimes called the wallet's map: the seeds are the keys to the doors, and the descriptor tells you which doors are yours.

Reading a descriptor

Descriptors are standardised in BIP 380 and the BIPs that follow it, and Bitcoin Core documents them in its descriptors guide. Here is a 2-of-3 one, shortened (so its checksum is only an illustration):

wsh(sortedmulti(2,[f00d1234/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6E.../<0;1>/*,[ab12cd34/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6F.../<0;1>/*,[99887766/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6D.../<0;1>/*))#q7k2s9xm

Piece by piece:

  • wsh( … ): "witness script hash", the native segwit wrapper for scripts (BIP 382). Addresses start with bc1q on mainnet.
  • sortedmulti(2, …): a multisig script needing 2 signatures from the keys listed, which are sorted into a fixed order for each address (BIP 383). Sorting means the order you list the keys in doesn't change the addresses.
  • [f00d1234/48h/0h/0h/2h]: the key's origin. f00d1234 is the master fingerprint of the device or seed it came from, a short ID that helps match keys to devices. 48h/0h/0h/2h is the derivation path, here the BIP 48 path for a native segwit multisig account on mainnet. The h means "hardened", the same as '.
  • xpub6E...: the extended public key for that account. It can produce public keys and addresses, never signatures.
  • /<0;1>/*: which addresses to derive. 0 is the receive chain, 1 the change chain, and * means "every index: 0, 1, 2…". The <0;1> form puts both chains in one line (BIP 389); older software writes two descriptors instead, one ending /0/* and one /1/*.
  • #q7k2s9xm: an eight-character checksum (BIP 380). If a character is mistyped when the descriptor is copied by hand, the checksum no longer matches and software refuses it, rather than silently building the wrong wallet.

Everything in that line is public information. That's what makes it safe to copy and keep in several places, with one important caveat.

The privacy caveat

A descriptor can't spend, but it can see. Anyone who reads it can derive every address of the wallet, then look them up on a block explorer to see your balance and every payment in and out. That's a reason to keep it private, not to keep it scarce. The descriptor's risk is privacy. Losing it costs you access. Weigh those two the other way round from seed words: spread descriptor copies widely enough that one always survives, but only where people you trust can see them.

How to back it up

A practical plan for a 2-of-3:

  1. Keep a copy with each key's backup. If your seed words are in three places, put a copy of the descriptor in all three. Then any two locations you can reach hold two seeds and the map.
  2. Use paper, and a digital copy if you like. Print it, ideally with a QR code of the same text, since several hundred characters are tedious to type. An encrypted file in your own storage works too. Paper is not encrypted, so store it where the privacy caveat above is acceptable.
  3. Write the first receive address next to it. After an import, the wallet should show that exact address first. If it shows a different one, something is wrong (a typo, a different script type, a missing key) and nothing should be sent to it.
  4. Label it in plain words. "This is the map of our 2-of-3 bitcoin wallet. It cannot spend. Two of the three keys are also needed." Your heirs may not know what wsh(sortedmulti(…)) means.
  5. Update it if the wallet changes. Replacing a key makes a new wallet with a new descriptor. Retire the old copies once the coins have moved, so nobody restores the wrong one.

Some tools package the descriptor with extra setup details in a standard file. BIP 129, "Bitcoin Secure Multisig Setup", describes such a format for registering and backing up a multisig wallet. If your software offers an export of that kind, it's a good thing to keep alongside the plain descriptor.

Why your heirs need it most

You might remember, years from now, which wallet app you used and roughly how it was set up. Your heirs won't. They will arrive with an inheritance letter, two devices or seed phrases, and no idea of script types or derivation paths.

With the descriptor, the job is mechanical: import it into wallet software that supports multisig descriptors (Bitcoin Core does, through importdescriptors, as its descriptors guide shows), check that the first address matches, connect two of the keys, and sign. Without it, they may need specialist help, and some combinations of lost information can't be recovered at all.

That is why a good inheritance plan names the descriptor explicitly and says where every copy is. Bitcoin inheritance without a company walks through the rest of such a plan. If you're still deciding on a setup, 2-of-3 multisig explained covers how the keys and pairs work. If a key is already missing, lost your hardware wallet, phone or seed phrase? covers what to do first.

What not to do

  • Don't put seed words in the same file as the descriptor, encrypted or not. The descriptor is meant to be spread around. Seeds are not.
  • Don't rely on a single app's cloud account as the only copy. Accounts get closed, apps get discontinued, and passwords get forgotten. Keep at least one copy you can read without any particular app.
  • Don't edit a descriptor by hand to "fix" it. If the checksum fails, find a better copy.
  • Never paste a descriptor, or anything else about your wallet, into a website offering to "recover" or "check" your coins. A descriptor alone can't steal anything, but it tells a scammer exactly how much you hold and makes you a target.

How Trikey handles the descriptor

Trikey is an open-source 2-of-3 wallet in which you hold all three keys. Its wallets are plain wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) descriptors on BIP 48 paths, the same form as the example above, so any multisig-capable wallet can import one and recover the coins with two keys, without Trikey (design decisions). The wallet core writes descriptors with the BIP 389 <0;1> form and the BIP 380 checksum.

Trikey keeps the descriptor wherever a key's backup is:

  • The phone's backup is an encrypted file holding key 2 and the descriptor, opened with a recovery code you keep (mobile app).
  • In Recovery Key mode (no home server), the printed Recovery Kit includes the descriptor for other wallet software, next to a QR code and the words that rebuild it (Recovery Key mode).
  • For the optional Savings wallet, the app prints a one-page wallet map: the checksummed descriptor as text and as a QR code, each key's device, fingerprint, path and xpub, and the first receive address to check an import against. The page holds no secret, and it says so, along with the privacy warning above (Savings).

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Try it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you use mainnet anyway, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide explains how.

FAQ

Is a wallet descriptor the same as an xpub?

No. An xpub is one key's public half. A descriptor combines one or more xpubs with the script, paths and threshold, so it describes the whole wallet. A multisig descriptor contains several xpubs.

Can someone steal my bitcoin with my descriptor?

No. It contains only public keys. They can see your balance and history, which is why you should keep it private, but they can't sign anything.

I only have a single-sig wallet. Do I need the descriptor?

It helps but is rarely essential, since wallets check the standard single-key paths when you restore a seed. Writing down the script type (for example "native segwit, BIP 84") does most of the job.

What if I lost the descriptor but still have all three seeds?

Then you can usually rebuild it: each seed gives its xpub at the usual multisig path, and you can try the common script types until the first address matches your records. It's slower and needs care, which is why a saved copy is worth having.

How many copies should I keep?

At least one with each key's backup, so any set of locations that holds enough keys also holds the map. More copies cost you privacy, not security.

item.title: Single-Sig or Multisig: When Is One Key Enough?
item.description: Singlesig vs multisig for bitcoin: what one key protects and what it doesn't, the questions that decide when a second and third key are worth it, and the costs.
item.content:encoded:
Most people who hold their own bitcoin start with one key: a hardware wallet or a phone app with a 12- or 24-word seed phrase. Sooner or later they read that "serious" holders use multisig, and wonder whether they should switch. This post answers that question without assuming the answer. One key is enough for many people and many amounts. The goal is to show where the line is, so you can tell which side of it you are on.

What one key means

A single-sig wallet ("single signature") can spend with one signature from one key. In practice that key comes from a seed phrase, usually in the BIP 39 format, and most modern wallets derive native segwit addresses from it along the BIP 84 path. Whoever holds the seed holds the money.

A multisig wallet needs several signatures from a set of keys, for example any 2 of 3. Each key lives on its own device or in its own place, and Bitcoin itself checks that enough of them signed. If you want the mechanics first, 2-of-3 multisig explained walks through them.

The difference that matters for the rest of this post: in single-sig, one secret decides everything. In multisig, no single secret does.

What a single key protects well

A single-sig wallet on a good hardware wallet, with a seed backup written down and kept safe, already handles the most common threats:

  • Malware on your computer. The key stays on the device, and the device shows the address and amount before you approve.
  • An exchange failing. Coins in your own wallet don't depend on anyone's solvency.
  • A lost device. Buy a new one, enter the seed, and the coins are back.
  • Simplicity. One backup, one device, and any standard wallet can restore it. Simplicity is a real security property: the setup you understand is the one you'll restore correctly in five years.

It also costs the least to use. A native segwit single-sig input is about 68 virtual bytes, against about 105 for a 2-of-3 P2WSH input, according to Bitcoin Optech's transaction size calculator (checked November 2026). Every payment you make from a coin pays for that difference in fees.

Where one key falls short

The weakness of single-sig is not that the key is weak. It is that everything rests on it, in two opposite directions.

It can be lost. If the device breaks and the seed backup is gone (a fire, a flood, a sheet thrown away by someone who didn't know what it was), the coins are gone. No one can reset it.

It can be found. Anyone who sees the seed phrase, photographs it, or tricks you into typing it somewhere can take everything, at once and for good. There is no waiting period and no second approval. The same is true of someone who holds your unlocked device and your PIN.

Notice the tension. The usual fix for "it can be lost" is more copies of the seed. The usual fix for "it can be found" is fewer copies, better hidden. A single key forces you to trade one risk against the other, and every copy you add for safety is one more place a thief can look.

A BIP 39 passphrase (sometimes called a "25th word") splits the secret into two items, so a found seed alone is not enough. It helps, but whoever learns both still holds a complete key, and losing the passphrase loses the coins just as surely as losing the seed.

What multisig changes

A 2-of-3 wallet resolves that tension rather than trading inside it. You can lose any one key and still spend with the other two. Someone can find any one key and still not be able to spend. Both statements hold at the same time, which no single key can offer.

It also changes the shape of an attack. A thief now needs two things from two places. A mistake, like leaving one backup in a hotel safe, is survivable instead of final.

But multisig is not "single-sig, only safer". It moves risk around:

  • More to back up. Besides each key's seed, you need the wallet's descriptor: the record of all the public keys and the script. Without it, the seeds you hold may not find the coins.
  • More steps to restore. Restoring takes two keys and the descriptor, in wallet software that supports multisig. People who never rehearse it can get stuck.
  • More ways to undo the benefit. Two keys kept in one drawer are one point of failure again, with more complexity on top.
  • Higher fees, as above, and a spend that reveals a multisig script on-chain.

So the honest question is not "is multisig better?" It is "would losing or leaking my one key hurt more than the cost of running three?"

Five questions that decide it

Answer these for the amount you are thinking about, not for your whole net worth.

1. Would losing this amount change your life?

If losing it would hurt but not change how you live, a well-backed-up single key is a reasonable place for it. If it would change your plans, your housing or your retirement, the case for removing the single point of failure is strong.

2. Who else knows, or could find out?

Single-sig is safest when nobody knows you hold bitcoin and nobody shares your home with your backup. Housemates, a public profile, renovations, or a past exchange account in your name all raise the chance that one secret is seen. Multisig makes one seen secret harmless.

3. Can you keep three things in three places?

Multisig only pays off if the keys really are apart: one at home, one in another building, one on a device that travels with you, or similar. If you cannot think of three sensible places, you will likely end up with two keys together, and you are better off with one key done well.

4. Will you rehearse a recovery?

Any setup you have never restored is a guess. Single-sig rehearsal is quick: wipe a spare device, enter the seed, and check the first address. Multisig rehearsal takes an afternoon. If you won't do it, keep the setup simple enough that you'd manage without practice.

5. Does someone else need to get in one day?

Heirs and family are where single-sig is weakest. Handing someone a seed phrase today gives them full control today. Multisig lets a family member, a lawyer's safe or a second location hold a key that can't spend alone, and, together with the descriptor, lets the right two keys open the wallet later. Bitcoin inheritance without a company covers that plan.

If most of your answers point to "small, private, simple", one key is enough. If most point to "large, known, shared", multisig is worth its costs.

Many people end up with both

The choice doesn't have to be all or nothing. A common pattern is a spending wallet with one key, holding what you'd carry in a physical wallet, and a vault behind several keys, holding the rest. The spending wallet stays fast and cheap. A thief who gets into your phone gets that much and no more, and the vault stays untouched. Refill the spending wallet from the vault now and then, when you can check the amount on a hardware wallet's screen.

Whatever you choose, the basics apply to both:

  • write the seed (and the descriptor, for multisig) on paper or metal, never in a photo, email or cloud note;
  • never type a seed into a website, and never share it with anyone who asks, whatever they claim to be;
  • check receive addresses on the device's screen before you share them;
  • rehearse a restore with a small amount before you trust the setup with a large one.

Where Trikey fits

Trikey is an open-source 2-of-3 wallet in which you hold all three keys: a hardware wallet, your phone, and either the Trikey Guardian on your own home server or a printed Recovery Key. The vault is a plain wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) descriptor on BIP 48 paths, the multisig script every major hardware wallet can co-sign, so any multisig-capable wallet can recover it with two keys (design decisions).

It is designed around the trade-off in this post: the convenience of one key for small, daily payments, and multisig for the rest.

  • With a home server, the phone pays alone up to a daily limit you set, because the guardian co-signs those payments. Larger payments, and any loosening of the rules, need the hardware wallet (rules the guardian enforces). Recovering from a lost phone waits out a delay with daily alerts, which Delay & Notify explains.
  • Without a home server, Recovery Key mode gives the phone a separate single-key spending balance, refilled from the 2-of-3 vault by a chain of payments the phone and hardware wallet pre-sign, at most one refill per period, enforced by Bitcoin's timelock rules (Recovery Key mode). The spending balance is exactly the "one key is enough" pocket described above, and it restores in any BIP 84 wallet.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Try it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you use mainnet anyway, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide explains how.

FAQ

Is a hardware wallet with one seed safe enough?

For many people and many amounts, yes, if the seed backup is written down, kept private and tested. Its limit is that one lost or seen backup decides the outcome. If that risk worries you more than added complexity does, consider multisig for the larger part.

Is a passphrase as good as multisig?

They protect different things. A passphrase stops someone who finds only the seed, but it is one more secret to lose, and anyone with both items can spend. Multisig survives a lost key and a stolen key at once, at the cost of more backups and steps.

Can I move from single-sig to multisig later?

Yes. You set up the multisig wallet, check its addresses on each device, and send your coins to it. That is an ordinary on-chain payment with an ordinary fee. Keep the old seed until the move has confirmed, then treat it as retired.

Does multisig protect me if someone forces me to unlock my keys?

Not by itself: if someone can make you use two keys, they can spend. Spending limits and waiting periods do more here, because they cap what can leave at once and give time to react.

What should I check when choosing devices for multisig?

That each device supports the script, lets you register the wallet, and shows the change and the address you're paying on its own screen. Choosing a hardware wallet for multisig covers the details.

item.title: Bitcoin Inheritance Without a Company: A Practical Plan
item.description: Bitcoin and crypto inheritance without a custodian: what heirs need, how multisig helps, the descriptor most plans forget, and the mistakes to avoid.
item.content:encoded:
If you hold your own bitcoin, nobody will hand it to your family when you die. There is no account to close and no bank to call. That is the point of self-custody, and it means the plan has to come from you. The good news is that a solid plan needs no company at all: it needs keys stored so that your heirs can gather enough of them and no thief can, the wallet's description written down, and plain instructions. This guide explains each part, how multisig makes it easier, and the mistakes that most often break a plan.

This is general information, not legal advice. Inheritance law differs by country; a lawyer can help with the legal side without ever touching your keys.

What your heirs will need

A workable plan answers five questions for the people you leave behind:

  1. That the bitcoin exists. Heirs cannot look for something they do not know about.
  2. Where enough keys are. For a single-key wallet, the seed phrase (and passphrase, if any). For a multisig, enough keys to meet the threshold.
  3. What wallet it is. For multisig, the descriptor: the public keys and how they combine. Without it, the keys may not find the coins.
  4. How to use it. Step-by-step instructions written for someone who has never done this, naming software that can import the wallet.
  5. Whom to trust. A person who can help, and a clear warning that anyone asking for seed words is a scammer.

Why single-key inheritance is hard

With one seed phrase, the same piece of paper that lets your heirs in also lets anyone else in. You have two bad options: keep it hidden so well that it may never be found, or tell people where it is and trust everyone who might learn it, for years.

Two specific traps:

  • Never put seed words in a will. In many jurisdictions a will becomes a public document once it goes through probate.
  • A passphrase helps security and hurts inheritance. If the passphrase lives only in your head, the seed alone opens an empty wallet.

How multisig changes the problem

A 2-of-3 multisig wallet splits the problem. No single location needs to be trusted, because one key alone moves nothing. A typical layout:

  • Key 1 at home, with you.
  • Key 2 with a trusted person, or in a safe deposit box.
  • Key 3 in a different place again: another relative, a second safe location, or a device you carry.

While you are alive, any one of those places can be burgled or lost without loss of funds. After your death, your heirs gather two of the three. The rule to keep: no single place, and no single person, should ever hold two keys.

The descriptor: the part most plans forget

Each key backup should come with a copy of the wallet's output descriptor. It looks like wsh(sortedmulti(2,[fingerprint/path]xpub…,…)) and lists all three public keys and the script type. It is standardised (BIP 380, BIP 383) and wallets such as Bitcoin Core, Sparrow and Nunchuk can import it.

Why it matters: two seeds out of three are not enough to rebuild a 2-of-3 wallet, because the wallet also needs the third key's public key to compute the addresses. With the descriptor, two seeds are enough.

The descriptor cannot spend, so storing a copy with each key does not weaken security. It does reveal your balance and history to whoever reads it, which is a privacy cost worth accepting here.

The letter of instruction

Write a letter that lives with your will or with a trusted person. It should say:

  • what you hold, roughly, and that it is bitcoin in self-custody;
  • where each key and each descriptor copy is, without the secrets themselves;
  • which devices or software to use, and that any multisig wallet that imports a descriptor will do;
  • who can help technically, and that they should never need to take the keys away;
  • that no legitimate helper, company or "recovery service" will ever ask for seed words;
  • that there is no rush: coins on the blockchain do not expire.

Keep secrets out of the letter: no seed words, no PINs, no passphrases. If PINs are needed (a hardware wallet wipes itself after too many wrong attempts), seed words restored on a new device avoid them; say where those seed words are instead.

Timelocked heir keys: the alternative

Some wallets built on miniscript add an heir path: your normal keys spend any time, and an heir's key can spend only after the coins have not moved for a set period (using Bitcoin's relative timelocks, BIP 112). The heir never needs your keys.

The trade-off: the timer counts from when each coin was confirmed, so you must move ("refresh") your coins before it runs out, every time, for as long as you live. Fewer hardware wallets can sign these scripts than plain multisig. We compare the approaches in Delay & Notify: why recovery should wait.

What companies offer, and what they change

Several collaborative custody companies (Casa, Unchained and Nunchuk among them) offer inheritance services that guide heirs through a process, usually with the company holding a key or playing a role in the recovery. That can be a good fit for families who want someone to call. It also makes the plan depend on the company still existing, and on its process, when the time comes. Check each provider's current documentation for exactly how theirs works. If you use one, keep your own copy of the descriptor so two of your own keys can always recover without it. We compare these models fairly in collaborative custody compared.

Common mistakes

  • Two keys in one place. A safe deposit box with two hardware wallets is a single point of failure, and a single target.
  • No descriptor copy. The most common way a multisig plan fails.
  • Instructions only you understand. Test them by asking someone non-technical to read them.
  • Never rehearsed. Do a dry run with a small amount: restore two keys on spare devices, import the descriptor into another wallet, and spend.
  • Never updated. Review once a year, and after you move house, change devices or change wallets.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey has no dedicated inheritance feature today. It is a 2-of-3 wallet where you hold all three keys (a hardware wallet, your phone, and the Trikey Guardian on your own home server), and several of its choices make the plan above easier:

  • A standard descriptor. Every wallet is a plain wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) on BIP 48 paths, and the phone's backup holds it. Any multisig-capable wallet can recover the coins with two of your keys, without Trikey, so your heirs do not depend on the project still existing.
  • A pair that needs no server. The phone key and the hardware wallet together can move any amount without the guardian. The phone key comes back from an encrypted backup file plus a recovery code written on paper, which the app tells you to keep apart: your letter should say where each is.
  • A printed recovery code with no secret on it (the guardian's address and relays), meant to be kept with the hardware wallet.
  • Alert contacts. If anyone starts a recovery, the people you chose are told every day and any of them can cancel it, which also protects a family during a confusing time.
  • A printed wallet map for the optional Savings wallet, built so that "the owner or an heir can find and recover Savings with its keys alone, without Trikey" (Savings).

The design document lists an opt-in timelocked heir path for miniscript-capable devices as a possible extra; it is not built, and the default stays plain multisig so that every hardware wallet can sign. The reasons are in the design decisions.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); do not build an inheritance plan on it for real funds yet. The testers guide explains how to try it.

FAQ

Can I leave my seed phrase in my will?

You should not. In many places a will becomes public during probate, and many people handle it before your heirs do. Say in the will where to find instructions, not the secrets.

What does an heir need to recover a 2-of-3 multisig?

Two of the three keys (seeds or working devices with their PINs) and the descriptor. With those, any multisig wallet that imports descriptors can move the coins.

Should my lawyer hold a key?

A lawyer can hold one key of a multisig without being able to spend, which is safer than holding a seed. Make sure they understand what it is and never hold a second key.

Is a company-assisted inheritance plan safer?

It is easier for some families and adds a party who can help. It also adds a party your plan depends on. Whichever you choose, keep your own descriptor so your keys alone can always recover.

How often should I review the plan?

Once a year, and whenever you change devices, wallets or where keys are stored.

item.title: Address Poisoning and Clipboard Malware: Limit the Damage
item.description: How address poisoning, clipboard malware and phishing trick people into sending bitcoin to attackers, how to check addresses, and how a daily limit caps losses.
item.content:encoded:
Many bitcoin losses involve no stolen keys at all. The owner signs the payment themselves, to an address that looks right and is not. Clipboard malware swaps the address you copied, address poisoning plants a lookalike in your history, and phishing gets you to hand over your seed or approve something you did not mean to. Bitcoin payments cannot be reversed, so the defence has two layers: check addresses in ways these tricks cannot fake, and set up your wallet so that when a check fails anyway, the damage has a ceiling. This article covers both.

Three ways to pay the wrong person

Clipboard malware ("clippers")

Malware on a computer or phone watches the clipboard. When you copy something that looks like a bitcoin address, it replaces it with the attacker's address. You paste, the wallet shows a valid address, and you send. Clippers often arrive with pirated software, fake apps and unofficial downloads.

Address poisoning

An attacker creates an address whose first and last few characters match one you use, which is cheap to generate, and gets it into your transaction history, usually with a tiny transaction. Later you copy "the usual address" from your history and pick theirs. Poisoning is most common on networks where people reuse one address for years, but it works anywhere people copy addresses from history or check only the ends.

Phishing

Fake support accounts, fake wallet websites, fake apps in app stores, emails about "wallet validation" or an urgent firmware update: the goal is either your seed words or a payment you did not intend. A variant targets wallets with security alerts: a fake "suspicious activity, click here to cancel" message.

How to check an address properly

  • Check the whole address, or a long stretch in the middle. Attackers match the beginning and the end because that is what people check. Read the full address, or compare a chunk of eight or more characters from the middle as well.
  • Check it on a screen malware cannot change. A hardware wallet shows the destination on its own display when you sign. Compare that with the address the recipient gave you through another channel, not with your computer's screen.
  • Do not copy addresses from your transaction history. Get a fresh address from the recipient each time, or use a saved contact you verified once.
  • Prefer QR codes and payment links (BIP 21 bitcoin: URIs) scanned from the recipient's own screen, which skip the clipboard.
  • Use a new receive address for every payment you receive. It keeps your history harder to poison and is better for privacy (see address reuse).
  • Send a small test payment first for large or first-time transfers, and confirm with the recipient that it arrived.

How to recognise phishing

  • No legitimate person or company ever needs your seed words. Not support, not a wallet maker, not a "recovery" service. Anyone who asks is stealing.
  • Install wallets only from the official source and check signatures where the project publishes them.
  • Firmware updates come through the vendor's own app or device, never through a link in a message.
  • Treat urgency as a warning sign. "Act within 24 hours" is how phishing gets past careful people.
  • Know what your wallet's real alerts look like. If its genuine alerts never contain links, a message with a link is fake.

Why verification is not enough on its own

Everyone fails a check eventually: a tired evening, a convincing message, a device that was already compromised. A good setup assumes that and limits what one mistake, or one compromised device, can cost:

  • A daily limit on the convenient path. Payments from your phone alone (or with an automatic co-signer) are capped per day. A clipper, a phisher or a thief who controls the phone can take at most the limit.
  • A stronger device above the limit. Larger payments need a hardware wallet, whose screen shows the real destination and amount. Malware on the phone cannot change what the device displays.
  • Rules that only the stronger device can loosen. If the phone alone could raise the limit, malware would simply raise it first.
  • Alerts and delays for unusual actions, such as a recovery starting (see Delay & Notify).
  • A separate wallet for savings that the everyday keys cannot touch.

A limit does not help if you approve a large payment to the wrong address on your hardware wallet yourself. That is why the device's screen, read carefully, remains the last check. Choosing a hardware wallet for multisig covers what a good device shows when it signs.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey is built around the second layer. It is a 2-of-3 multisig wallet with your hardware wallet (key 1), your phone (key 2) and the Trikey Guardian on your own home server (key 3). From the design document's rules and threat model:

  • A daily limit you set (the app suggests 200,000 sats). The guardian co-signs phone payments only while the total leaving the wallet over a rolling 24 hours, fees included, stays under it. A stolen or compromised phone can send at most that.
  • Over the limit, the hardware wallet signs instead of the guardian, and shows the payment on its own screen.
  • Raising the limit needs the hardware wallet. The phone alone can only tighten the rules. The approval is a short text the device displays, with the new values in clear.
  • Turning the limit off is possible but strictly opt-in: it needs its own hardware approval, and your alert contacts are told. With the limit off, a thief who gets into the phone can send everything at once, and the design says so.
  • Alerts never carry a link or a button and never ask anyone to sign in, in any channel. The guardian breaks up anything link-like before it sends a message, so a message with a link is not from it.
  • The Recovery Kit's words are never put on the clipboard. The phone backup's recovery code can be copied, because the alternative people use is a screenshot that photo galleries sync and keep. The copy is marked sensitive on Android, kept local on iOS, and taken back after 60 seconds; the screen says that an app reading the clipboard in that minute could see it, and paper stays the advice. On Android both are hidden from screenshots and the app switcher.
  • An optional Savings wallet that the phone and the guardian cannot move even together.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide includes a payment inside the limit and one over it, so you can see both paths.

FAQ

Can I get bitcoin back if I sent it to a poisoned address?

Almost never. Bitcoin payments cannot be reversed. Report it to the police if the amount matters, and beware of "recovery" services that contact you afterwards: they are a common second scam.

Does a hardware wallet protect against clipboard malware?

Only if you read the address on the device's screen and compare it with the recipient's real address. The device shows what it signs; it cannot know who you meant to pay.

Is checking the first and last characters enough?

No. Lookalike addresses are generated to match exactly those. Check the whole address, or a long section in the middle as well.

What is a good daily limit?

Enough for what you spend from your phone in a normal day, and small enough that losing it would hurt but not matter. You can lower it at any time; raising it should need a stronger key.

How do I know an alert from my wallet is real?

Learn what your wallet's real alerts contain. If they never include links or ask you to sign in, any message that does is fake. When in doubt, open the wallet app yourself rather than following the message.

item.title: Choosing a Hardware Wallet for Multisig: What Matters
item.description: What matters when a hardware (cold) wallet joins a multisig: wallet registration, address and change checks, PSBT, message signing and connections.
item.content:encoded:
Almost every bitcoin hardware wallet can sign for a multisig wallet. Far fewer can protect you inside one. In a 2-of-3 multisig, the hardware wallet is usually the key that stops a compromised phone or computer, so what matters is not the logo but what the device checks and shows on its own screen. This guide lists the features worth looking for, why each one matters, and the questions to ask before you buy. It does not crown a winner: firmware changes often, so check each vendor's current documentation for the features below.

Why multisig asks more of a hardware wallet

With a single-key wallet, the device knows everything about the wallet: it holds the only key. In a multisig, it holds one key of three and has to trust the other two public keys it is told about. If malware on your computer or phone can swap one of those public keys, it can make "your" multisig addresses belong partly to the attacker, or make "change" go somewhere you do not control. BitBox's engineers described these attacks in detail in how nearly all personal hardware wallet multisig setups are insecure, and several vendors improved their firmware afterwards.

The features below are what close those gaps.

1. The script types you plan to use

Check that the device signs the multisig script your wallet uses. Native segwit multisig (P2WSH, usually on BIP 48 paths) is the most widely supported. Taproot multisig and miniscript policies (timelocks, heir paths) are supported by fewer devices. If you want a timelocked recovery path, confirm support first.

2. Wallet registration

Registration means the device is shown the whole multisig wallet once (all public keys, the threshold, the script type), you approve it on the device's screen, and the device remembers it (or a proof of it). After that:

  • it can show you receive addresses and confirm they belong to this wallet;
  • it can recognise change going back to the same wallet, and show it as change rather than as a payment;
  • a swapped public key produces a different wallet, which the device does not recognise.

Some devices store the wallet; others keep a short proof that the host sends back each time, as Ledger's Bitcoin app does with an HMAC. Some devices are stateless and rely on the details sent with each request. Ask how a device without registration verifies your cosigners and your change.

The BSMS standard (BIP 129) and output descriptors (BIP 380) are common ways to hand a wallet to a device; what a wallet descriptor is explains what one contains.

3. Address verification on the device's screen

Before receiving a large amount, show the address on the hardware wallet and compare it with what your phone or computer shows. If malware changed the address on the computer's screen, the device's screen will not match. Look for:

  • the full address on screen, not a shortened one;
  • a check that the address belongs to the registered multisig, not just that it contains the device's own key;
  • for best protection, the same address shown on two different devices.

4. Clear payment review

When you sign, the device should show every output's address and amount, the fee, and which outputs are change. If it cannot recognise change, it will show change as a payment to an address you cannot check by eye, and you lose the ability to spot a swap, the attack described in address poisoning and clipboard malware.

5. PSBT support and how it connects

Multisig transactions travel between signers as PSBTs (BIP 174). How the PSBT reaches the device is a trade-off:

ConnectionStrengthsTrade-offs
USBSimple, fastNeeds a cable and a compatible port
BluetoothWorks with phonesA wireless link to secure and pair
QR codesAir-gapped, phone-friendlyLarge transactions need animated QR codes
NFCTap to send, no cablePhone support varies (iPhone apps need extra permissions)
microSD cardAir-gapped, any sizeSlow; files can linger on cards and computers

None is "the secure one". What matters is that the device shows and checks everything itself, whatever the channel.

6. Message signing at multisig paths

Some multisig wallets use the hardware wallet for more than payments: to approve a rule change, pair with a co-signer or prove ownership. They do it by asking the device to sign a short text with a key it controls, typically as a BIP 137-style signed message (or the newer BIP 322).

If a wallet you plan to use needs this, check three things:

  • Which key paths the device will sign a message with. Some firmware only signs messages with single-key paths, or refuses multisig account paths.
  • How much text it shows. A device that cuts the text after a fixed number of characters may hide the part you need to read.
  • That it shows the text at all. A device that signs a message without displaying it is signing blind.

7. Protection against malicious firmware

A device with tampered firmware could, in theory, leak its key through the random values in its signatures. Some devices (for example the BitBox02 and Blockstream's Jade) support an anti-exfil or anti-klepto protocol in which the phone or computer contributes randomness and checks that the device used it. Also worth weighing: open-source firmware, reproducible builds, and how firmware updates are verified.

8. Mixing brands

In a multisig, using devices from different vendors means one vendor's bug or supply-chain problem affects only one key. The cost is learning two or three interfaces. Many people consider it worth it.

A short checklist

  • Does it sign my wallet's script type?
  • Can I register the multisig and approve it on the device?
  • Does it show full receive addresses and confirm they belong to the registered wallet?
  • Does it recognise change?
  • How does it connect to the phone or computer I will use?
  • If my wallet needs message signing, will it sign at the paths it needs, and show the whole text?
  • Is the firmware open source and reproducible?

How Trikey approaches it

In Trikey, the hardware wallet is key 1: it approves payments over your daily limit, every loosening of the rules, pairing with the guardian, and recovery access for a new phone. That puts more weight on the features above than a plain multisig does. From the design document's hardware wallets by feature:

  • Script: plain wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) on BIP 48 paths, chosen because every major device can co-sign it.
  • Registration and address check: the wallet is registered on devices that need it (Ledger, BitBox02, Jade, Coldcard), and the vault's first address is shown on the device for you to compare, for every device.
  • Approvals are signed messages (BIP 137) of at most 240 characters, which show the new rules in clear, so you read them on the device's screen. Texts that name your alert contacts are kept within what the Jade displays before it truncates.
  • Connections: Ledger over Bluetooth; Trezor through Trezor Suite Lite; Jade by QR or Bluetooth; BitBox02 over USB-C on Android (the Nova also over Bluetooth); Coldcard Q by QR, and Coldcard Mk4 or Q over NFC; Keystone 3, Passport Prime and Specter DIY by QR; Passport (2nd generation) and Krux by QR for payments and microSD for signed messages.
  • SeedSigner signs payments but refuses messages at the multisig path Trikey's approvals use, so it works for payments and Recovery Key mode, not as the hardware wallet of a guardian wallet.
  • Anti-klepto is used with the BitBox02 for payments and most texts.

The most important caveat: only the Ledger has been tested on real hardware so far. Support for every other device was written from its firmware's source code and official clients and is untested on devices. If you own one, a hardware wallet test report on a test network is one of the most useful things you can contribute, even if everything works; the testers guide explains how to set up.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet, use only an amount you can afford to lose.

FAQ

Can I use any hardware wallet in a multisig?

Most current devices can sign standard P2WSH multisig. Whether they can register the wallet, verify addresses and recognise change varies, and those are what protect you.

Do I need three hardware wallets for a 2-of-3?

No. Many setups use one or two hardware wallets plus a phone key or a co-signing service. What matters is that the keys live in different places and no single device or place holds two.

Is an air-gapped hardware wallet safer for multisig?

Air-gapping removes a cable or wireless link, but the main protection in multisig is what the device verifies and shows. An air-gapped device that cannot recognise change is weaker than a connected one that can.

Why does my hardware wallet show a "register wallet" screen?

It is asking you to approve the multisig wallet's keys once. Compare what it shows with your wallet software (and ideally your other devices) before approving.

What does message signing have to do with multisig?

Nothing for payments. Some wallets use signed messages to let the hardware wallet approve non-payment actions, such as changing a spending limit. If yours does, the device must sign at the right path and show the whole text.

item.title: Collaborative Custody Compared: Who Holds the Third Key?
item.description: Bitkey, Casa, Unchained, Nunchuk and DIY multisig compared fairly: who holds which key, what each key can do, and what happens if a company goes away.
item.content:encoded:
"Collaborative custody" means a 2-of-3 multisig wallet in which you hold two keys and a company holds the third. It sits between handing your bitcoin to an exchange and carrying every key alone. Several good products work this way, and they differ in what the company's key is allowed to do. This article compares the main models by the question that matters most: who holds the third key, and what can that key do? It is written to be fair: each model has real strengths, and the right choice depends on what you want help with.

Product details change. Everything below is taken from each provider's public documentation as of November 2026; check their current pages before deciding.

The four models

1. An exchange or custodian holds everything

The simplest option: the company holds the keys, and you hold an account. Recovery is a password reset. The trade-off is that the bitcoin is the company's to move, freeze or lose, and your access depends on its solvency and its policies. Not self-custody, but worth naming as the baseline.

2. You hold one key (single-sig)

One hardware wallet and one seed phrase. Fully yours, simple and cheap, and every company could disappear without effect. The risk is that the seed is a single point of failure for both loss and theft (see what happens if you lose a key).

3. You hold two keys, a company holds one

The collaborative model. No party can spend alone: not you with one key, not the company with its key. What the company's key does varies:

  • A recovery key. The company signs only to help you after you lose a key. Day to day, you spend with your own two keys.
  • A co-signing key with rules. The company's server co-signs everyday payments from your phone, within limits, so you do not need your hardware wallet for small amounts. It also runs a delayed recovery.

4. You hold all three keys

Do-it-yourself multisig with a coordinator such as Sparrow, Nunchuk, Specter or Electrum, and three hardware wallets or seeds kept in different places. No company in the loop at all. The trade-off is that you are your own support desk, and everyday spending means fetching two devices.

The providers, briefly

Bitkey (Block)

A 2-of-3 with three fixed roles: an app key on your phone, Bitkey's own hardware device, and a server key held by Block. Block's server co-signs with your phone up to a daily limit you set, so small payments do not need the hardware. Over the limit, the hardware device signs. If you lose a key, Delay + Notify recovers it after a seven-day waiting period with alerts, and you can cancel a recovery you did not start. An Emergency Exit Kit lets you move your funds with your phone key and hardware key without Block's servers. The roles are fixed: you cannot swap in another hardware wallet or a different cosigner.

Good fit for: people who want everyday phone payments with a hardware backstop and a company that runs the server.

Casa

A 3-key vault (2-of-3) in which you hold a mobile key and a hardware key, and Casa holds the Casa Recovery Key. Casa's documentation says it holds only that key and cannot move funds with it alone; it exists to help you recover when you lose access to one of your keys. Casa also documents recovering without Casa (for example in Sparrow) and offers larger vaults and inheritance services.

Good fit for: people who want a guided setup, a recovery partner and support, with day-to-day spending on their own keys.

Unchained

A 2-of-3 vault in which you hold two keys (usually two hardware wallets) and Unchained holds one. Unchained's key acts as a backup and recovery key. Its help pages describe external recovery: spending from the vault with your two hardware wallets, the wallet configuration file and another multisig wallet (Caravan or Sparrow), without the Unchained platform. It also offers larger quorums, inheritance and financial services built around the vault.

Good fit for: larger holdings, people who want a long-term custody partner and an established company behind it.

Nunchuk

A wallet app that does both: fully self-managed multisig (every key yours) and assisted wallets, in which Nunchuk holds a Platform Key. Its documentation describes using that key for day-to-day co-signing and spending limits, on paid plans. It also offers inheritance planning.

Good fit for: people who want one app that can start self-managed and add a company key later.

Side by side

ExchangeSingle-sigCompany holds 1 of 3You hold 3 of 3
Who can spend aloneThe companyYouNobodyNobody
A single lost keyAccount resetFunds at risk without backupRecover with the other twoRecover with the other two
Phone-only everyday paymentsYesDepends on the walletWith a co-signing service (Bitkey, Nunchuk assisted)Not usually
Help when things go wrongSupport deskNoneSupport deskNone, or a friend
If the company disappearsDepends on the companyNothing changesYou still hold two keys; keep the wallet configurationNothing changes
What the company seesEverythingNothingUsually your wallet's addresses and transactionsNothing

What a company key gives you, honestly

  • Someone to call. Setup help, a recovery process and, for families, an inheritance process.
  • An always-on co-signer for phone payments, without running any hardware yourself.
  • Accountability. A company with a reputation and a legal identity.

What it costs

  • Fees. Most collaborative plans are subscriptions.
  • Dependence for what the key does. If the company stops, its features stop; your two keys still recover, as long as you kept the wallet configuration.
  • Privacy. A co-signer that checks your payments must see them, and usually knows your whole wallet.
  • Fixed choices. Some products fix the hardware or the roles; others let you choose.

None of these is a flaw in a particular company. They are the shape of the model.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey keeps the everyday shape of the co-signing model, phone payments within a daily limit and a waiting-period recovery with alerts, and gives the third key back to you. The co-signer, the Trikey Guardian, is an app on your own home server (Umbrel, Start9, or a computer or NAS running Docker); a bitcoin co-signer on your home server explains what that protects. The design document says it plainly: no company runs a server, a guardian or a cosigner for anyone.

  • Key 1: a hardware wallet of your choice (Ledger, Trezor, Coldcard, Jade, BitBox02, Keystone, Passport, Krux or Specter DIY), not one brand.
  • Key 2: your phone. With the guardian, it pays within your daily limit.
  • Key 3: your guardian, which co-signs only within the rules your hardware wallet approved, and runs a 7, 14 or 30-day Delay & Notify recovery.
  • Recover anywhere: a plain wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) descriptor, so any multisig wallet can move the coins with two of your keys.

What you give up compared with a company: there is no support desk, you keep a home server running, and if it goes offline, phone-only payments wait (your phone and hardware wallet still move any amount). A remote compromise of your home server gives up one key of three, the same exposure as a company's co-signing server being breached (threat model). And unlike the products above, Trikey is not a finished product.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide explains how to try it. Trikey is an independent open-source project and is not affiliated with any of the companies named here.

FAQ

What is the best Bitkey alternative?

It depends on what you like about Bitkey. For a company-run co-signer with phone payments, look at assisted multisig such as Nunchuk's. For a recovery partner with your own two keys, Casa or Unchained. For no company at all, do-it-yourself multisig, or a self-hosted co-signer such as Trikey once it is ready.

Can the company in collaborative custody take my bitcoin?

Not alone: it holds one key of three, and the wallet needs two. It could refuse to sign, which is why you should always be able to spend with your own two keys.

What happens to my funds if the company shuts down?

You still hold two keys. With the wallet's configuration (descriptor) and any multisig wallet, you can move the funds. Save that file today and test it once.

Is collaborative custody still self-custody?

Most people count it as such, because no single party, the company included, can move the funds. You hold the majority of the keys.

item.title: A Bitcoin Co-Signer on Your Home Server: What It Protects
item.description: What running a bitcoin node and a co-signing key on Umbrel, Start9 or Docker protects against, what it does not, and how to run one safely at home.
item.content:encoded:
Home servers such as Umbrel and Start9 made it easy to run a Bitcoin node in a box on a shelf. Most people use one to check their own transactions and keep their addresses private. A newer idea goes one step further: let the box hold one key of a 2-of-3 multisig wallet and co-sign payments under rules you set, the way a company's server does in collaborative custody. This article explains what a home node protects, what a home co-signer adds, what neither protects against, and how to run one without creating new risks.

What your own node already gives you

You check the chain yourself

A wallet has to learn which coins you own and whether a payment confirmed. Without a node, it asks someone else's server, and trusts the answer. With your own node, your wallet asks software you run, which has checked every block itself.

Your addresses stay private

Most mobile and desktop wallets look up addresses through an Electrum server. A public one learns every address you ask about, and usually your IP address too, so it can link your whole wallet together. Umbrel and Start9 offer Electrum server apps (such as Electrs or Fulcrum) that run next to Bitcoin Core, so your wallet can ask your own box instead.

You broadcast your own transactions

Sending through your own node means no third party sees a payment before the network does.

What a node does not do on its own: hold keys or enforce any rule about spending. That is the co-signer's job.

What a co-signer on the box adds

A co-signer is a key that signs only when a request meets its rules. Companies run them for collaborative custody (see collaborative custody compared). Running one at home gives you the same kinds of rules without a company holding a key:

  • A spending limit. Your phone plus the co-signer can pay up to a daily amount. Above it, the hardware wallet must sign. A stolen phone is worth at most the limit.
  • A waiting period for recovery. If you lose a key, the co-signer helps you recover, but only after a delay with alerts (see Delay & Notify).
  • Rules that only a stronger key can loosen. Raising the limit or shortening the delay needs the hardware wallet, not just the phone.
  • Alerts to you and people you trust when something unusual happens.

A few open-source projects explore self-hosted co-signers with policies, such as Ledger's resigner and Coinkite's CKBunker; check each project's repository for its status and intended use.

What it does not protect against

Being honest about the limits is the most useful part of this article.

A compromised box is one key of three

If someone takes over your home server remotely, they hold the co-signer's key. In a 2-of-3 wallet that is one key: not enough to spend. It is the same exposure as a company's co-signing server being breached. But it means the co-signer must never be your only line of defence: someone holding the box and one of your other keys holds two keys.

Burglary

A burglar who takes your phone and your home server has two of your three devices. If they keep the box running and its rules hold, that buys them the daily limit, and any recovery they start sets off the alerts. If they unplug it, a good design makes the server lock itself on restart (a key encrypted on disk is useless without its passphrase), so the box is worthless. Either way, keep your hardware wallet's seed words outside your home: the hardware wallet plus the phone would be a pair with no limit.

Downtime

Power cuts, internet outages, a failed disk or an update gone wrong all stop the co-signer. A design worth trusting keeps your money reachable without it: in a 2-of-3, your phone and hardware wallet are still a spending pair.

Other apps on the same box
